rejected.title: Common access resources
card: A common access resource is rival and non-excludable. Rival means one person's use leaves less for others. Non-excludable means it is hard to stop people using it.
Examples are ocean fish stocks, groundwater in a shared aquifer and open grazing land. Where there are no enforced limits or property rights, users do not pay for what they take.
Each user gains the full benefit of taking more, but shares the cost of a smaller stock with everyone else. So each has little reason to hold back.
The result is overuse. The resource can run down or be depleted, and this is a market failure. The market output is above the social optimum.
rejected.remember: Rival but hard to exclude: users take too much and the resource runs down.

a.q: Which resource is a common access resource?
opts: Fish in an unregulated ocean fishery
Street lighting in a country town
Grapes grown in a private vineyard
A cinema seat booked and paid online
a.why: Fish are rival, as each fish caught is gone, and it is hard to stop boats fishing in open waters with no limits. Street lighting is non-rival, as one person's use leaves the same for others, so it is not a common access resource.
a.clue: Look for a resource that runs down when used and has no gate.

b.q: In a region with no limits on pumping, dozens of farmers draw water from one shared aquifer. Why is the aquifer likely to be overused?
opts: Each farmer gets the full gain but shares the depletion cost
Each farmer pays the full social cost of the water they pump
Water is non-rival, so pumping leaves the same for others
Farmers can easily be excluded, so they rush to pump more
b.why: Each farmer keeps the full benefit of extra water, while the cost of a falling water level is spread across all users. So each pumps more than the social optimum. The non-rival option is wrong because water one farmer pumps is gone for the others.
b.clue: Think about who gets the gain and who shares the cost.

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'Water in the aquifer is rival, so the third option is wrong.' The third option is the intended right answer. The non-rival option it means to rule out is listed first, so the why contradicts the answer it explains.

The stem puts the scenario near Mildura and says 'Nobody can be stopped from pumping.' In Victoria, groundwater is vested in the Crown and extraction needs a licence under the Water Act 1989, so this is not true of a real Australian aquifer. The question should use a hypothetical setting or say it is unregulated.

'Nobody owns them' is loose for the Australian context. Groundwater is Crown-owned and regulated, and Australian ocean fisheries are managed with licences and quotas. The point being taught is the lack of enforceable property rights or limits on use, not literal ownership.
